mainEntity.name: How long should a dental crown typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental crowns are designed to be long-lasting restorations, and many function well for ten to fifteen years or more with appropriate care. However, longevity varies depending on the material used, the location of the crown in the mouth, the patient's bite, and oral hygiene habits. Regular professional monitoring and good home care can help maximise a crown's lifespan. No crown lasts indefinitely, and your dentist will advise you when replacement is clinically appropriate based on examination and X-ray findings.

mainEntity.name: Can a dental crown develop decay underneath it?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, secondary or recurrent decay can develop at the junction between a crown and the natural tooth, particularly if the cement seal has weakened or the crown margin has become exposed over time. Because this area is covered, decay in this location may not cause obvious symptoms initially. This is one of the reasons regular dental check-ups, including X-rays where appropriate, are important for patients with crowns, as decay beneath a crown can be identified before it becomes more extensive.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if my crown feels loose?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your crown feels mobile or you suspect it may have partially dislodged, contact your dental practice to arrange an assessment. Avoid applying excessive force to the crown in the meantime. Do not attempt to re-cement a crown yourself using over-the-counter products without first discussing this with your dentist. A loose crown leaves the underlying tooth structure vulnerable and requires professional evaluation to determine the most appropriate course of action. Temporary measures may be available in some circumstances, but these should be discussed with your clinician.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal for a crowned tooth to feel sensitive?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some sensitivity immediately following crown placement is not unusual as the tooth and surrounding tissues settle. However, sensitivity that develops weeks or months after a crown has been in place, or sensitivity that is increasing in intensity, should be assessed by a dentist. This may indicate that the crown's fit has changed, that decay is present beneath the restoration, or that the tooth's nerve is affected. Sensitivity alone does not always indicate a serious problem, but it merits professional evaluation to determine the cause.

mainEntity.name: Can a chipped crown be repaired without full replacement?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, minor chips to a porcelain or ceramic crown can be smoothed or repaired, depending on the size and location of the chip and the material involved. In other cases, a full replacement crown may be the more clinically appropriate option. The decision depends on an assessment of the structural integrity of the existing crown and the underlying tooth. Your dentist will advise you on the most suitable approach following a thorough examination. Leaving a chipped crown unaddressed is generally not recommended, as rough edges may harbour bacteria or cause irritation.

mainEntity.name: How often should dental crowns be professionally reviewed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Crowns should be assessed at every routine dental examination, which for most patients means at least once a year, though your dentist may recommend more frequent reviews depending on your individual circumstances. X-rays may be taken periodically to check for changes beneath the crown that are not visible clinically. If you have multiple crowns, or if you have been identified as someone who grinds their teeth, your dentist may recommend additional monitoring. Early detection of any changes allows for timely intervention and helps to protect the long-term health of the tooth.
